seasonalFood.title: Seasonal Food of the Month
seasonalFood.description: See which Korean vegetables, fruits and seafood are in season each month, with tips on choosing, storing and cooking them from Korea's Rural Development Administration and Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries.
seasonalFood.descriptionMonth: In {m}, {veg} vegetables, {fruit} fruits and {sea} kinds of seafood are in season. Check how to pick and store them before you shop.

seasonalFood.seafoodTip: Keep seafood at 5°C or below in the fridge or -18°C or below in the freezer, rinse it 2–3 times under running water before cooking, and cook it through where possible (Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries).

deodeok.name: Deodeok (bonnet bellflower root)
deodeok.pick: White, thick, straight roots with a strong aroma
deodeok.keep: Wrap in damp newspaper and keep in the vegetable drawer (around 10°C) so it doesn't freeze

minari.name: Minari (water dropwort)
minari.pick: Bright green, stems not too thick, leaves of even length
minari.keep: Wrap in newspaper, put in a bag and store upright in the fridge
minari.dish: Seasoned minari, steamed pork belly with minari

doraji.name: Doraji (balloon flower root)
doraji.pick: Soil and fine roots still attached, strong aroma; Korean roots are white once peeled
doraji.keep: Unpeeled, wrapped in newspaper, in a cool airy place

bomdong.name: Bomdong (spring cabbage)
bomdong.pick: Fresh leaves, not too large, with a yellow heart
bomdong.keep: Seal in a plastic bag and refrigerate so it doesn't dry out

naengi.name: Shepherd's purse (naengi)
naengi.pick: Dark green leaves and a strong scent; avoid thick, tough roots
naengi.keep: Wrap in cling film and refrigerate for 2–3 days; blanch any leftovers

cabbage.name: Cabbage
cabbage.pick: Firm and heavy with glossy pale-green outer leaves; avoid heads that give when pressed
cabbage.keep: Cut out the core, fill it with damp paper towel, wrap in film and refrigerate

dallae.name: Wild chive (dallae)
dallae.pick: Fresh stems and neat bulbs; very large bulbs are less flavourful
dallae.keep: Roll in newspaper, put in a bag or box and refrigerate
dallae.dish: Dallae soy dipping sauce, seasoned dallae

mugwort.name: Mugwort (ssuk)
mugwort.pick: Young, tender leaves; plump with a reddish base
mugwort.keep: Blanch and freeze, or dry well and keep in an airy place

dureup.name: Fatsia shoots (dureup)
dureup.pick: About 12–15 cm, fragrant, tender shoots with leaves not yet open
dureup.keep: Don't wash; mist lightly, wrap in newspaper and refrigerate in a sealed box. Blanch and freeze to keep longer
dureup.dish: Blanched dureup with chojang, dureup skewers

bambooShoot.name: Bamboo shoots
bambooShoot.pick: Green, tightly attached husks; brown husks mean it was dug long ago
bambooShoot.keep: Flavour fades fast after harvest, so boil before storing
bambooShoot.dish: Bamboo shoot salad, bamboo shoot rice

spinach.name: Spinach
spinach.pick: Thick, glossy dark-green leaves and bright red roots
spinach.keep: Wrap unwashed in paper towel and store upright in the fridge, away from apples and kiwis

tomato.name: Tomato
tomato.pick: Fresh green stem, firm and heavy for its size
tomato.keep: At room temperature out of sunlight in an airy place
tomato.dish: Stir-fried tomato and eggplant, tomato salad

gondre.name: Gondre (thistle greens)
gondre.pick: Dark green leaves with no damage or insect holes; dried gondre should be evenly greenish brown
gondre.keep: About 2 days in the fridge; blanch and freeze, or dry it, to keep longer

onion.name: Onion
onion.pick: Firm, heavy, with dry papery skin; avoid sprouting onions
onion.keep: Don't seal; hang in a mesh bag in a cool airy place

potato.name: Potato
potato.pick: Smooth with few blemishes, heavy and firm; avoid sprouted or green potatoes
potato.keep: In a box or newspaper away from light in an airy place; an apple in the box slows sprouting

eggplant.name: Eggplant
eggplant.pick: Deep glossy purple, firm and straight

corn.name: Corn
corn.pick: Bright green husks that aren't dry, with full dark-brown silk
corn.keep: Sweetness fades after picking, so steam once and freeze in portions

yeolmu.name: Young radish greens (yeolmu)
yeolmu.pick: Fresh light-green leaves; short, young plants with plump stems
yeolmu.keep: Wrap in newspaper and refrigerate base-down for 2–3 days; blanch and freeze to keep longer

zucchini.name: Korean zucchini (aehobak)
zucchini.pick: Even thickness end to end, bright pale green and glossy
zucchini.keep: Wrap in newspaper and refrigerate; slice and dry, or blanch and freeze, to keep longer
zucchini.dish: Zucchini pancakes, zucchini and shrimp pancakes

pepper.name: Green chili pepper
pepper.pick: Dark green, smooth and springy when pressed; avoid dried stems
pepper.keep: Best around 7°C; colder makes the inside turn black. Slice and keep in a container for longer storage
pepper.dish: Braised green chilies, stuffed chili kimchi

lotusRoot.name: Lotus root
lotusRoot.pick: Straight and heavy, not dry outside, white inside with evenly sized holes
lotusRoot.keep: Peeled lotus root browns quickly, so soak it in vinegar water and refrigerate
lotusRoot.dish: Braised lotus root, lotus root pancakes

shiitake.name: Shiitake mushroom
shiitake.pick: Caps moderately open, gills underneath intact, stems short and plump
shiitake.keep: Don't wash; wipe with a dry cloth, wrap in film and freeze

taro.name: Taro
taro.pick: Long oval shape, white once peeled
taro.keep: Not in the fridge: wrap with soil on in damp newspaper and keep somewhere cool (10–15°C)
taro.dish: Taro soup, taro and perilla soup

oldPumpkin.name: Ripe pumpkin (neulgeun hobak)
oldPumpkin.pick: Deep yellowish brown with a white bloom, round with deep ridges
oldPumpkin.keep: Out of direct sun in an airy place below 10°C; it keeps well at room temperature

napaCabbage.name: Napa cabbage
napaCabbage.pick: Thin, tender leaves, firm white ribs and a full yellow heart when cut
napaCabbage.keep: Somewhere cool; in the fridge, wrap in paper and store upright

radish.name: Korean radish (mu)
radish.pick: White, smooth, firm and heavy; avoid split radishes or ones with many fine roots
radish.keep: With soil on, wrapped in newspaper, out of sunlight; cut off the greens before refrigerating
radish.dish: Cubed radish kimchi, spicy radish salad

broccoli.name: Broccoli
broccoli.pick: Tight, domed florets of deep green
broccoli.keep: It can flower at room temperature, so blanch lightly and refrigerate
broccoli.dish: Blanched broccoli with chojang, stir-fried broccoli

ginger.name: Ginger
ginger.pick: Firm, large knobs with few wrinkles and a strong scent
ginger.keep: Wrap in a damp cloth and refrigerate for use within 2–3 days; for longer, wrap unwashed in newspaper

tangerine.name: Mandarin (gyul)
tangerine.pick: Thin skin hugging the flesh, flat shape, green stem; avoid overly shiny fruit
tangerine.keep: Spread on newspaper so they don't touch, in a cool airy place
tangerine.dish: Mandarin dressing salad, mandarin white kimchi

hallabong.name: Hallabong
hallabong.pick: Skin that isn't puffy or heavily wrinkled; puffy fruit tends to be bland or sour
hallabong.keep: At cool room temperature in an airy place

strawberry.name: Strawberry
strawberry.pick: Fresh green caps, glossy red all the way to the stem
strawberry.keep: Leave the caps on, cover with film and refrigerate; eat soon, as they mould easily

chamoe.name: Korean melon (chamoe)
chamoe.pick: Deep yellow, deep grooves and firm
chamoe.keep: About 3 days somewhere cool, or about 7 days washed and wrapped in the fridge

raspberry.name: Wild raspberry
raspberry.keep: Refrigerate and eat as soon as possible

mulberry.name: Mulberry (odi)
mulberry.pick: Black, plump, not mushy, with fresh stems
mulberry.keep: They soften fast, so seal unwashed and freeze

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.pick: Large, thin springy rind and clear dark stripes
watermelon.keep: Wrap cut melon fully in film over a plate and refrigerate; eat soon

peach.name: Peach
peach.pick: Evenly coloured, unblemished, fuzzy all over with a sweet scent
peach.keep: Wrap in newspaper somewhere cool; white peaches like 8–10°C, yellow peaches 3–5°C

melon.name: Melon
melon.pick: Fine, even netting; the heavier of two same-sized melons
melon.keep: Long refrigeration dulls the sweetness, so keep it at room temperature (20–25°C) for a few days

grape.name: Grapes
grape.pick: Dark colour, plump berries and white bloom intact; loose berries mean old fruit

blueberry.name: Blueberry
blueberry.pick: Deep blue, taut berries of even size with a white bloom
blueberry.keep: Dry well and keep in an airtight box in the fridge or freezer

pear.name: Korean pear
pear.pick: Clear yellow skin, smooth, with no bulge opposite the stem
pear.keep: Wrap and refrigerate, away from apples
pear.dish: Steamed pear with honey, pear salad

fig.name: Fig
fig.pick: Uncracked, evenly reddish brown, slightly soft when pressed, fresh stem
fig.keep: Best eaten right away; otherwise seal and refrigerate at 1–5°C, or make jam

plum.name: Plum
plum.pick: Firm, glossy skin and a stem that isn't dry

apple.name: Apple
apple.pick: Medium size, springy skin, even colour and a gentle scent
apple.keep: Apples soften other fruit, so wrap separately and keep cool or refrigerated

kiwi.name: Kiwi (chamdarae)
kiwi.pick: Dark brown skin and even shape; if slightly soft when pressed, it's ready to eat
kiwi.keep: Ripen hard kiwis at room temperature for a few days (faster with an apple), then refrigerate

persimmon.name: Persimmon
persimmon.pick: Sweet persimmons with no gap between calyx and fruit, unblemished and firm
persimmon.keep: Best at 0–2°C, so bag and refrigerate; wrap astringent ones in paper and keep somewhere cool for 2–3 weeks
persimmon.dish: Persimmon pickles, ripe persimmon rice cake

jujube.name: Jujube
jujube.pick: Dried jujubes that are glossy, clean, evenly wrinkled and don't rattle when shaken
jujube.keep: Wash, dry, pit, then seal in portions and freeze

yuzu.name: Yuzu
yuzu.pick: Unblemished, firm, bumpy skin with a strong scent and colour
yuzu.keep: Wrap whole in newspaper and refrigerate; use glass rather than metal containers for preserves

oyster.name: Oyster
oyster.dish: Oyster pancakes, maesaengi and oyster soup

maesaengi.name: Maesaengi seaweed
maesaengi.dish: Maesaengi and oyster soup, maesaengi pancakes

flounder.name: Marbled flounder (dodari)
flounder.dish: Flounder and mugwort soup, flounder sashimi

seaSquirt.name: Sea squirt (meongge)
seaSquirt.dish: Sea squirt bibimbap, sea squirt sashimi

webfoot.name: Webfoot octopus (jukkumi)
webfoot.dish: Seasoned webfoot octopus, stir-fried webfoot octopus

anchovy.name: Anchovy
anchovy.dish: Anchovy ssambap, spicy raw anchovy salad

blueCrab.name: Blue crab (kkotge)
blueCrab.dish: Spicy crab stew, steamed blue crab

abalone.name: Abalone
abalone.dish: Abalone porridge, abalone in soy sauce

seabass.name: Sea bass (nongeo)
seabass.dish: Sea bass sashimi, grilled sea bass

horseMackerel.name: Horse mackerel (jeongaengi)
horseMackerel.dish: Grilled horse mackerel, braised horse mackerel

croaker.name: Brown croaker (mineo)
croaker.keep: For sashimi, aging it 2–3 days in the fridge brings out its flavour and texture

gizzardShad.name: Gizzard shad (jeoneo)
gizzardShad.dish: Salt-grilled gizzard shad, spicy gizzard shad salad

spanishMackerel.name: Spanish mackerel (samchi)
spanishMackerel.dish: Salt-grilled Spanish mackerel, braised Spanish mackerel

why.title: Why seasonal food is cheaper and tastier
items: In season, crops are harvested and fish are caught in large volumes, so markets are well stocked and prices tend to fall.
Food harvested at full growth or peak fat has more flavour. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries notes that Spanish mackerel builds fat from autumn and is at its best from November through winter.
The same food tastes different by season. Nongsaro explains that radish harvested in autumn is crisper and sweeter than spring or summer radish.
It doesn't need long storage or long-distance shipping, so it reaches the table fresher.

house.title: Greenhouses, fish farms and seasons
items: Greenhouse crops such as strawberries and tomatoes are available most of the year. Even so, Nongsaro notes that strawberries grown in cold winter are sweeter and less sour than spring ones.
Spinach comes as 'winter spinach' grown in autumn and winter and 'summer spinach' grown in spring and summer. This page treats winter to early spring as its season.
Heavily farmed seafood such as abalone and black rockfish is sold all year, so cards also flag the ministry's pick for that month.
Kiwi, apples and pears are stored and shipped over a long period. Hayward kiwis are on sale from November to April.

shopping.title: Shopping tips for the month
items: Check 'How to pick' on each card while you shop. Heavy, firm and brightly coloured is usually best.
Greens you can't finish can be blanched, squeezed dry and frozen in single portions.
Apples give off a lot of ethylene, which softens nearby fruit and vegetables. Keep them away from quick-wilting greens like spinach.

Keep seafood at 5°C or below in the fridge or -18°C or below in the freezer and rinse it 2–3 times under running water. Cooking it through is safer than eating it raw (Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries).
In kimchi-making season (November–December), napa cabbage, radish and ginger are all in season together.

closed.title: Closed fishing seasons
closed.intro: During a closed season the species may not be caught. Frozen, farmed and imported products are still sold, but anglers and anyone catching their own must follow the rules.
items: Japanese flying squid: April 1 – May 31
Webfoot octopus: May 11 – August 31
Fleshy prawn: May 1 – June 30
Spanish mackerel: May 1 – May 31
Gizzard shad: May 1 – July 15 (except Gangwon and Gyeongbuk)
Mottled skate: June 1 – July 15
Blue crab: June 21 – August 20 (varies by sea area)
Hairtail: July 1 – July 31
Pen shell: July 1 – August 31
Abalone: September 1 – October 31 (Jeju: October 1 – December 31)
Marbled flounder: December 1 – January 31
closed.note: Based on Incheon City's guide to the Enforcement Decree of the Fishery Resources Management Act. Exceptions apply by sea area and fishing method, so check the National Law Information Center and local notices for exact dates.

method.title: How seasons are set on this page
items: Vegetables and fruit: months they appear in Nongsaro's 'Ingredient of the Month' (Rural Development Administration), plus harvest and shipping periods in Nongsaro's item notes.

Seafood: months chosen as the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries' 'Seafood of the Month' (2017–2026) and months listed in Nongsaro's 'Seafood of the Month'. A single isolated pick is left out, and every 2026 pick is included.
Gaps of two months or less between those months are filled in. Seasons can shift a month or two with region, weather and variety.
Mushrooms (shiitake) are listed with vegetables. Picking and storage tips are shortened from Nongsaro's item notes.

items.a: Napa cabbage, radish, ripe pumpkin, lotus root and ginger for vegetables; persimmon, yuzu, kiwi and jujube for fruit; and Spanish mackerel, scallops, cod, cockles and mackerel for seafood. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries chose Spanish mackerel and scallops as its November 2026 Seafood of the Month.

We combined the months each item appears in Nongsaro's 'Ingredient of the Month' and 'Seafood of the Month', the ministry's 'Seafood of the Month' picks (2017–2026) and harvest periods in Nongsaro's item notes. Region and weather can shift them by a month or two.
Strawberries are mostly harvested in greenhouses from winter to spring. Nongsaro notes that winter strawberries are sweeter and less sour than spring ones, so December–May is marked as their season.
The ministry picked oysters for December every year from 2019 to 2023, and Nongsaro features oyster pancakes as a January seafood dish, so December–January is marked as their season.

items.q: Can I eat a fish during its closed season?
items.a: Closed seasons restrict catching, so buying frozen, farmed or imported fish at the market is fine. If you fish or gather it yourself, you must follow the closed season and minimum size rules.

items.q: How do I keep greens longer?
items.a: Quick-wilting greens such as fatsia shoots, gondre and young radish greens can be blanched, squeezed dry and frozen in single portions. Gondre can also be boiled and dried in the shade to keep as dried greens.
